questions.prompt: How is a MOSFET's unity-gain frequency \(f_T\) defined?
options: The frequency where a CS amplifier's voltage gain falls to 1
The \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency of the device with its drain open
The frequency where the short-circuit current gain \(|i_{out}/i_{in}|\), drain AC-shorted, falls to 1
The frequency where \(C_{gs}\) and \(C_{gd}\) are equal
questions.explanation: Drive the gate with a current, short the drain to AC ground, and compare currents. Shorting the drain removes any load, so \(f_T\) is a property of the device and its bias alone (reader Sec. 14.10.1).

questions.prompt: A device has \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(C_{gs} = 48\ \mathrm{fF}\) and \(C_{gd} = 2\ \mathrm{fF}\). Find \(f_T\) in GHz.
questions.explanation: \(f_T = g_m/[2\pi(C_{gs} + C_{gd})] = 2\ \mathrm{mS}/(2\pi\cdot50\ \mathrm{fF}) = 6.37\ \mathrm{GHz}\). With the drain shorted, both capacitances hang on the gate. Leaving out \(2\pi\) gives the radian frequency, 40 Grad/s.
questions.figure_alt: Short-circuit current gain magnitude in dB versus log frequency: it falls at 20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB at the unity-gain frequency f_T.

questions.prompt: For a long-channel device, \(\omega_T \approx \tfrac32\mu_nV_{ov}/L^2\). Which change raises \(f_T\) the most?
options: Doubling \(W\)
Doubling \(V_{ov}\), which quadruples \(f_T\)
Halving \(C_{ox}\)
Halving \(L\), which quadruples \(f_T\)
questions.explanation: \(g_m \propto W/L\) and \(C_{gs} \propto WL\), so \(W\) and \(C_{ox}\) cancel and \(f_T \propto \mu V_{ov}/L^2\) (reader Eq. 14.64). Doubling \(V_{ov}\) only doubles it.
questions.figure_alt: Short-circuit current gain magnitude in dB versus log frequency: it falls at 20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB at the unity-gain frequency f_T.

questions.prompt: Using \(\omega_T = \tfrac32\mu_nV_{ov}/L^2\) with \(\mu_n = 400\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\,s)}\), \(V_{ov} = 0.2\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(L = 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) (overlap ignored), find \(f_T\) in GHz.
questions.explanation: \(\omega_T = 1.5(0.04\ \mathrm{m^2/(V\,s)})(0.2)/(0.5\times10^{-6})^2 = 4.8\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), so \(f_T = 7.64\ \mathrm{GHz}\). Forgetting to convert cm² to m² is off by \(10^4\).
questions.figure_alt: Short-circuit current gain magnitude in dB versus log frequency: it falls at 20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB at the unity-gain frequency f_T.

questions.prompt: At fixed \(W/L\), you double a device's bias current. How does \(f_T\) change (long-channel, capacitances unchanged)?
options: It rises by \(\sqrt2\), because \(g_m \propto \sqrt{I_D}\)
It doubles
It is unchanged
It halves
questions.explanation: The gate capacitance is set by geometry, so \(f_T\) follows \(g_m\). Doubling current at fixed size raises \(V_{ov}\) and \(g_m\) by \(\sqrt2\).

questions.prompt: Why is the output short-circuited when \(f_T\) is measured?
options: To make the drain current zero
So the result does not depend on any load, and \(C_{gd}\) is not Miller-multiplied
To put the device in triode
To remove \(C_{gs}\) from the circuit
questions.explanation: With \(v_{ds} = 0\), \(C_{gd}\) is simply another capacitance from gate to AC ground and the gain has no load in it. That makes \(f_T\) a fair figure of merit for comparing devices.

questions.prompt: A process has \(f_T = 5\ \mathrm{GHz}\) at \(L = 0.4\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). At the same overdrive, estimate \(f_T\) (GHz) for \(L = 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) using the long-channel scaling.
questions.explanation: \(f_T \propto 1/L^2\), so halving \(L\) gives \(4\times5 = 20\ \mathrm{GHz}\). Short-channel devices fall short of this because velocity saturation makes \(f_T \propto 1/L\).
questions.figure_alt: Short-circuit current gain magnitude in dB versus log frequency: it falls at 20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB at the unity-gain frequency f_T.

questions.prompt: A device has \(f_T = 10\ \mathrm{GHz}\) (\(C_{gd}\) negligible). What is its short-circuit current gain magnitude at 500 MHz?
questions.explanation: Above the gate's pole the current gain falls as \(f_T/f = 10\ \mathrm{GHz}/0.5\ \mathrm{GHz} = 20\).
questions.figure_alt: Short-circuit current gain magnitude in dB versus log frequency: it falls at 20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB at the unity-gain frequency f_T.

questions.prompt: Preview of the Miller effect: a CS amplifier built from a 10 GHz device, driven from a 10 kΩ source with a gain of 20, has a bandwidth far below 10 GHz. Why?
options: Because \(f_T\) is measured with an open drain
Because the gain is negative
The source resistance must charge \(C_{gs}\) plus a Miller-multiplied \(C_{gd}\)
It does not; the bandwidth equals \(f_T\)
questions.explanation: \(f_T\) assumes a current drive and a shorted drain. Real stages have source resistance and voltage gain, which put \((1 + A)C_{gd}\) on the input.

questions.prompt: Preview of cascades: as a rough rule, a single stage cannot have a gain-bandwidth product above about \(f_T\). With \(f_T = 20\ \mathrm{GHz}\), what is the best-case bandwidth (GHz) at a gain of 10?
questions.explanation: \(f_T/A = 20/10 = 2\ \mathrm{GHz}\). Real stages do worse; splitting gain across stages is one way to win bandwidth back.
questions.figure_alt: Short-circuit current gain magnitude in dB versus log frequency: it falls at 20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB at the unity-gain frequency f_T.

questions.prompt: Preview of follower bandwidth: why can a source follower approach the device's \(f_T\) more closely than a CS stage?
options: Because its gain is larger
Because it has no capacitances
Because its drain is at the supply, which removes \(C_{gs}\)
Its gate and source move together, so \(C_{gs}\) carries little current and there is no Miller multiplication of \(C_{gd}\)
questions.explanation: Bootstrapping leaves only \(C_{gs}(1 - A_v)\) on the input.
